items.followUp: Define an organ. Name the three types of muscle tissue and give one feature of each.

rubric.why: A tissue is defined by its similar cells working together for a function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a tissue consists of similar cells performing the same function.

rubric.why: Skeletal muscle is distinguished by voluntary control or attachment to bones.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming skeletal muscle and giving a correct feature.

rubric.why: Smooth muscle is involuntary and is commonly described as spindle-shaped.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming smooth muscle and giving a correct feature.

rubric.why: Cardiac muscle occurs in the heart and is involuntary.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming cardiac muscle and giving a correct feature.

modelAnswer: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform the same function.
Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and is under voluntary control.
Smooth muscle is found in the walls of internal organs and is involuntary.
Cardiac muscle is found in the heart and contracts involuntarily.

items.followUp: Define a catalyst and explain how an enzyme helps convert a substrate into products.

rubric.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts, generally proteins, that speed up reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining enzymes as biological catalysts or proteins that speed up reactions.

rubric.why: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site, which is specific to it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the active site and its specific substrate.

rubric.why: Binding forms the enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the enzyme and substrate form a complex.

rubric.why: The reaction converts the substrate into products, which leave the active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that products form and are released.

rubric.why: The enzyme remains unchanged and can catalyse another reaction.
rubric.description: States that the enzyme can be reused.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the enzyme is not used up or remains unchanged.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
A substrate with a suitable shape binds to the enzyme's specific active site.
This binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
The substrate is converted into products, which leave the active site.
The enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.

items.followUp: Describe how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: A limiting factor restricts the rate when it is in short supply or at an unsuitable level.
rubric.description: Explains the idea of a limiting factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that a limiting factor restricts the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity generally increases photosynthesis until another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking light intensity with the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; increased availability can raise its rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking carbon dioxide availability with the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled: temperature raises its rate up to an optimum, while excessive heat damages enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the temperature effect, including an optimum or the harmful effect of excessive heat.

modelAnswer: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by factors that are in short supply or at unsuitable levels.
As light intensity increases, the rate usually increases until another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration can increase the rate because carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum; excessive temperature can damage enzymes and reduce the rate.

items.followUp: Explain how guard cells cause stomata to open and close.

rubric.why: Guard cells surround and control the opening of each stoma.
rubric.description: Identifies the guard cells and their role.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that guard cells surround or control the stoma.

rubric.why: In light, guard cells take up water and become turgid.
rubric.description: Explains the change that opens the stoma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking water uptake and guard-cell turgidity with opening.

rubric.why: Turgid guard cells bend apart, opening the stoma.
rubric.description: Describes how turgid guard cells open the stoma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that turgid guard cells cause the opening to open.

rubric.why: When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid and the stoma closes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking water loss and flaccidity with closure.

modelAnswer: Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells that control its opening and closing.
In light, guard cells take up water by osmosis and become turgid.
The turgid guard cells bend apart, so the stoma opens.
When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid and the stoma closes; this commonly occurs in darkness.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a plant's root and flower in terms of their functions.

rubric.why: Roots, stems and leaves are the vegetative organs of a plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming roots, stems and leaves as vegetative organs.

rubric.why: Flowers and related reproductive structures are involved in producing offspring.
rubric.description: Identifies reproductive organs and their function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming flowers or other reproductive organs and linking them to reproduction.

modelAnswer: Vegetative organs include roots, stems and leaves; they perform functions such as absorption, support and food-making for plant growth.
Reproductive organs include flowers and the structures that form fruits and seeds; they take part in reproduction.

items.followUp: What are biomolecules? Name two major groups of biomolecules.

rubric.why: Biomolecules are chemical substances or molecules found in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biomolecules are chemical substances or molecules found in living organisms.

rubric.why: Examples or groups show what substances are included among biomolecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming two correct groups of biomolecules.

modelAnswer: Biomolecules are chemical substances found in living organisms.
Examples include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

items.followUp: Name two laws of inheritance proposed by Gregor Mendel.

rubric.why: The law of segregation is a recognised biological law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the law of segregation.

rubric.why: Independent assortment and dominance are recognised Mendelian laws.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a second correct biological law.

modelAnswer: Two examples of biological laws are Mendel's law of segregation and law of independent assortment.

items.followUp: Define bioinformatics and name one type of biological information it can analyse.

rubric.why: Bioinformatics applies computer methods to biological information or data.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking computers or computer science with biology or biological data.

rubric.why: Analysing biological data, such as DNA or protein sequences, is a key use of bioinformatics.
rubric.description: States the data or purpose of bioinformatics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a biological data type it analyses or stating that it analyses biological information.

modelAnswer: Bioinformatics is the use of computers and information technology to collect, store and analyse biological information.
It can be used to analyse DNA or protein sequences.
